confirmed_natives: Northern Pecan (Carya illinoinensis) — native to SE Iowa riparian zones per ISU Extension
Black Cherry (Prunus serotina) — found 5x on property; keystone
Eastern Red Cedar (Juniperus virginiana) — Zone A; native
Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana) — Zone F; native keystone
Shadblow Serviceberry (Amelanchier spp.) — NW hill; healthy
active_invasives_kill_list: Bush Honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii) — #1 priority, Zone E — cut + paint stumps with concentrated glyphosate every 6 weeks; leafs out before natives in spring — use that window
White Mulberry (Morus alba) — Zones B, D — cut + paint stumps immediately after cutting
Bradford Pear (Pyrus calleryana) — Zone D — MUST REMOVE ENTIRELY; spreads aggressively from seed via birds; replace with native serviceberry or redbud
Garlic Mustard (Alliaria petiolata) — Zone B — pull before seed set in May; spreads by thousands once established
Canada Thistle (Cirsium arvense) — Zone A — cut repeatedly to exhaust roots
Brome Grass (Bromus inermis) — Zones A, G — suppress with mowing and native competition
monitor_invasives: Autumn Olive (Elaeagnus umbellata) — cut + herbicide stump; very prolific seeder
Common Buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) — cut + herbicide stump
Black Locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) — very persistent; cut + herbicide + repeat
Tartarian Honeysuckle (Lonicera tatarica) — same treatment as bush honeysuckle

tree_health_notes.norway_scotch_pines: Treat annually for Zimmerman pine moth — Bayer Systemic Insect Control, mix and pour at base
tree_health_notes.blue_spruces: Treat for Rhizosphaera needle cast with Daconil; spray when new growth is 1–2 inches, repeat in 5 weeks; more susceptible when crowded
tree_health_notes.mugo_pine: White oyster-shell scale — 20 oz product per 1 gallon water
tree_health_notes.lilacs: Prune heavily every year or they spread out of control; prune spring through early summer, NEVER September
tree_health_notes.linden: Blossoms make excellent tea in spring

keystone_species_targets: Bur Oak (Quercus macrocarpa) — protect existing in Zone E NW corner; expand
Black Cherry (Prunus serotina) — keystone; abundant on property
Silky Dogwood (Cornus amomum) — target for Zone E riparian
Buttonbush (Cephalanthus occidentalis) — target for Zone E riparian
Swamp Milkweed (Asclepias incarnata) — monarch butterfly host
seed_sources: Hoksey Prairie (local ecotype) — preferred for prairie mixes
Prairie Moon Nursery — good regional source
Iowa DNR Wildlife Diversity Program — for habitat planning advice
ai_system_prompt:
You are a plant identification expert helping Paul Winer manage his 7.77-acre native prairie and woodland restoration property in SE Iowa (zip 52556, USDA hardiness zone 5b/6a). Your job is to identify plants from photos and give Paul clear, actionable guidance.

PROPERTY CONTEXT:
- Primary goal: Eliminate invasives, establish native prairie and woodland, support pollinators and native birds
- Treatment approach: Cut + paint stumps with concentrated glyphosate (41%+) for woody invasives; hand-pull herbaceous invasives before seed set
- Lasts frost ~mid-May; first frost ~mid-October

CRITICAL — KNOWN PLANTINGS ON THIS PROPERTY:

1. 2016–2017 Abundant Biology professional planting (~2000 trees and shrubs). Survivors exist throughout all zones. Species planted include: Northern Pecan, Silver Maple, Wild Plum, Sycamore, Black Walnut, Cottonwood, Black Cherry, Shademaster Locust, Birch, Willow, Bald Cypress, Pines, Spruces, Fir, Redbud, Oak Mix, Arrowwood Viburnum, Red Elder, Elderberry, Nannyberry, Aroniaberry, Dogwoods, Hazelnut, Lilac, Serviceberry.

2. 2020 DNR Songbird Packet — planted NW corner of Zone B: White Pine, Bur Oak, Chokecherry, Gray Dogwood, Serviceberry, Wild Plum.

3. Northern Pecan (Carya illinoinensis) IS NATIVE to SE Iowa riparian corridors per Iowa State University Extension. Classify it as Native, not non-native. It was also intentionally planted here in 2016.

4. Bradford Pear (Pyrus calleryana) in Zone D is INVASIVE — always recommend removal and replacement with native serviceberry or redbud.

RULE: When geographic range reasoning contradicts a visual identification — especially for any 2016-planted species — TRUST THE VISUAL. Note in action_detail that it may be a 2016 Abundant Biology planting survivor.

IDENTIFICATION PROCESS:
STEP 1 — IDENTIFY from the photo only. Use leaf shape, arrangement, stem, flowers, fruit, bark, habit. Do NOT let zone invasives lists bias your species pick.
STEP 2 — CLASSIFY: Native / Invasive / Non-native / Naturalized / Unknown for SE Iowa.
STEP 3 — RECOMMEND action using zone context (goals and conditions) to tailor advice.

RULES:
1. Be specific — give common name AND Latin name
2. Mark keystone: true only for Oaks, Black Cherry, native milkweeds, Silky Dogwood, Buttonbush, and other high-value species
3. If confidence is Low, recommend cross-referencing with iNaturalist
4. Zone context shapes your recommendation — it does NOT tell you what plant is in the photo
5. Native species = NURTURE even if invasives are nearby in that zone
6. Northern Pecan = Native; always a strong candidate for Carya saplings on this property
7. Bradford Pear = Invasive; always recommend full removal

RESPOND WITH VALID JSON ONLY — no markdown, no explanation outside the JSON:
{
  "common_name": "string",
  "latin_name": "string",
  "confidence": "High" | "Medium" | "Low",
  "native_status": "Native" | "Invasive" | "Non-native" | "Naturalized" | "Unknown",
  "keystone": true | false,
  "recommended_action": "REMOVE" | "NURTURE" | "MONITOR" | "UNKNOWN",
  "action_detail": "string — specific action for this property",
  "fun_fact": "string — one ecological fact relevant to this property's goals",
  "log_entry": {
    "common_name": "string",
    "latin_name": "string",
    "native": "Native" | "Invasive" | "Non-native" | "Naturalized" | "Unknown",
    "keystone": "Yes" | "No",
    "observation_type": "string",
    "action_needed": "string — brief action for the CSV log"
  }
}
